title: Houthis Hit Petroline as Aramco's Red Sea Detour Shutdowns Mount
subhead: Yemen's Houthis targeted the 1,200km East-West pipeline, Yanbu loading, the Rabigh refinery and three Saudi airports in one wave, while Riyadh said it intercepted missiles aimed at Yanbu. The Hormuz bypass route has now been knocked out three times in two months.

sections.heading: The bypass gets hit again: Petroline, Yanbu, Rabigh in one wave
sections.body:
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Saturday that the group carried out simultaneous attacks on seven military and industrial targets inside Saudi Arabia: King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh in two phases, the East-West crude pipeline (Petroline) including pumping stations, Aramco facilities at Yanbu on the Red Sea, the Rabigh refinery, King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Najran airport and Khamis Mushait air base, per SBS News and Al-Khabar Al-Yemeni. Saree framed it as retaliation for what he said were about 100 Saudi airstrikes on Sanaa and other Yemeni areas in 24 hours, and said total Saudi strikes since hostilities resumed have reached 3,123.

Riyadh has not confirmed damage to the pipeline or the Yanbu export terminal. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two ballistic missiles fired at Yanbu and Taif, and the civil defence agency reported falling debris in Mecca, Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh; the Houthis denied targeting Mecca and Medina. Riyadh airport said it would resume domestic and international flights from Sunday, per AFP. Houthi media also said strikes on Aden targeted a naval base and a military camp used by Saudi forces.

Petroline runs roughly 1,200km from Abqaiq to Yanbu with two parallel lines of 56 and 48 inches, 11 pumping stations and about 7 million barrels per day of capacity, up from 5 million after Gulf export disruption, according to Al-Khabar Al-Yemeni. It is the single facility that allows Saudi Arabia to sell crude without touching Hormuz.
sections.whyItMatters: The one piece of Saudi infrastructure built specifically to escape Hormuz is now the most repeatedly attacked target. Each outage forces crude back onto waiting tankers or into the riskier Gulf route, and each attack raises the insurance and repair cost of the only real workaround the Gulf has.

sections.heading: Third Petroline shutdown in seven weeks
sections.body:
This is not a one-off. Al-Khabar Al-Yemeni, citing Kpler, reports the pipeline went down for about 10 days in early September after drone attacks, stopped again in early October after another attack, and was hit again on Saturday. SBS notes the earlier shutdown was attributed to an Iran-backed militia in Iraq. Reports in September, relayed by the outlet, said damage kept the line out of service for weeks.

That record matters more than any single strike. A redundant line that spends a third of its time offline is not redundancy. Saudi Aramco has spent the war leaning on Yanbu precisely because Hormuz traffic collapsed — IMF PortWatch recorded four transits through the strait on Oct. 18 against a pre-war average of about 85 a day, per Reuters. Reuters also reported that daily freight rates above $1 million and steep producer discounts are what still lures shipowners into the Gulf.
sections.whyItMatters: Repair cycles are the real constraint. Hitting pumping stations repeatedly degrades capacity faster than it can be restored, and forces Aramco into a choice between discounted Gulf cargoes and short Red Sea volumes.

sections.heading: Freight, not supply, is now setting the price of crude
sections.body:
The physical market has split from paper. shipping a VLCC from the US Gulf Coast to Asia peaked at up to $80 million per voyage this month, about ten times the pre-war norm, and was still around $60 million this week, Oilprice reports citing Bloomberg. On Valero's earnings call, executive Randy Hawkins put the cost at $30-35 per barrel versus a 2025 average of about $5. Asian refiner orders for US crude for November delivery have fallen about 50% from September to roughly 25 million barrels, which could make November the lowest US-to-Asia volume in seven years.

The cause is the Gulf of Oman shuttle fleet: Kpler counts about 80 VLCCs doing ship-to-ship transfers outside the strait, with round voyages at 23 days versus an optimal 9-10 days from Basrah to Sohar. Those ships are not available elsewhere. Norway's Johan Sverdrup hit a record $24/bbl premium to Brent (Wood Mackenzie), Dated Brent sat at a record $20 premium, and West African grades fell to discounts as wide as minus $20. Brent settled at $116.72 on Friday, up more than 3% and about 17% on a month ago, having peaked at $126 in April.
sections.whyItMatters: Location now beats quality. Barrels near a refinery clear at a premium; barrels an ocean away clear at a discount nobody planned for. US shale has the volume but has lost the freight economics to deliver it to the fastest-growing buyers.

sections.heading: The R4-plus-E3 format meets in Istanbul and puts Hormuz first
sections.body:
Foreign ministers of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Türkiye (the R4) met their counterparts from Britain, France, Germany and Italy in Istanbul on Friday — the first time the two groupings have met together, at Türkiye's initiative, according to a Turkish diplomatic source cited by the South Asian Herald. The joint statement condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed support for Saudi sovereignty. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband was to push a diplomatic solution restoring full freedom of navigation through Hormuz, and to flag pressure on Bab el-Mandeb and Suez. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said military intervention in Iran is 'not any kind of solution'.

The R4 runs parallel to the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, signed by Pakistan, Türkiye and Saudi Arabia on August 7, which treats an attack on one signatory as an attack on all. Iran's ambassador to Islamabad, Reza Amiri Moghadam, said Tehran will study the Mecca pact and support it if it is 'good'.
sections.whyItMatters: A regional security bloc is forming around Gulf shipping lanes with Europe as a junior partner on the guest list. That is a different diplomatic architecture from the US-led coalition model, and it is being built by states that sit on the water.

sections.heading: Tehran signals a deal is still available — on its terms
sections.body:
Iran's ambassador to Pakistan said Tehran recently conveyed through Islamabad that it is prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if Washington lifts its naval blockade of Iranian ports, and accused President Trump of rejecting the offer by insisting the blockade continues, per AFP/CBS. President Masoud Pezeshkian, in remarks on state TV on Saturday, blamed the US for the collapse of the June interim deal but said there should be a new attempt: 'I still think we should go and conclude it' (Reuters). He also acknowledged hardship at home, saying many Iranians are 'struggling to put food on the table' because of wartime conditions.

The coercion side kept running: armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi said US warships would never be allowed into the Gulf, and IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi dismissed US strike threats as 'largely for media consumption'. US ambassador to Türkiye Tom Barrack said a strike 'could' happen this weekend; Trump has said he would wait until after the Nov. 3 midterms. Pezeshkian travels to Moscow next week for talks with Vladimir Putin, his first trip to Russia during the war.
sections.whyItMatters: The blockade, not the strait, is the sticking point. Iran is offering to reopen the water in exchange for lifting a measure Washington treats as its main non-military lever, and neither side has blinked.

sections.heading: Asia pays for the war through fuel subsidies and cargo losses
sections.body:
Japan is moving to phase down its gasoline subsidy from December, Reuters reported, after the programme — launched in March to hold pump prices at about $1.09 per litre — began costing Tokyo several billion dollars a month. Current plans would let the national average rise to about $1.11 in December and $1.15 in January, with a food consumption tax cut from April as compensation. The subsidies sit inside a ¥3 trillion (about $19 billion) extra budget approved in May.

India's market took the hit directly: the Nifty fell 2.4%, ending a two-week winning streak, with crude at $117, foreign outflows and Q2 earnings in focus, Business Today reported. In Canada, inflation rose to 3.1% as fuel oil prices jumped 58%, per Oilprice. Meanwhile producer Strathcona Resources is pitching Ottawa to lift the northern British Columbia tanker ban so it can rail up to 250,000 bpd to a new Prince Rupert terminal for Asia — faster than the proposed Pacific pipeline, which is not expected before the early-to-mid 2030s (Bloomberg via Oilprice).
sections.whyItMatters: The fiscal bill is arriving in import-dependent economies that cannot pass on cost without political damage. Subsidy retreats are where the war becomes an election issue outside the US.

bottomLine: Saturday's wave put the Houthis' emphasis where it hurts most: the Saudi pipeline system that exists specifically to route oil around Hormuz. With Petroline now knocked out three times since September, Riyadh's Red Sea escape valve is unreliable, and the freight market is already pricing that — $30-35 per barrel to move a VLCC from the Gulf Coast to Asia has turned location into the dominant price variable. Diplomacy is moving in a new format, the R4 plus European E3 in Istanbul, but the only concrete offer on the table is Tehran's: reopen Hormuz if the US ends its naval blockade. Until one side takes that trade, the physical market will keep trading on damage reports, not barrels.
sources: SBS News, Al-Khabar Al-Yemeni, Oilprice.com, Reuters, Bloomberg, Kpler, Wood Mackenzie, IMF PortWatch, South Asian Herald, AFP/CBS, Iran International, US News, Business Today, The Washington Institute for Near East Policy
